flashcards.q: What does Dynamo do mechanically, and how does that differ from torch.jit.script?
flashcards.a: Dynamo hooks CPython's frame evaluation API to trace real, unmodified eager code as it runs, capturing an FX graph plus runtime guards. torch.jit.script required rewriting code into a restricted, statically-analyzable subset ahead of time, which broke on dynamic control flow Dynamo handles via graceful graph breaks.

flashcards.q: What is a guard, and what happens when one fails?
flashcards.a: A cheap runtime check (shape, dtype, device, certain Python values) that must hold for a captured graph to be safely reused. A guard failure triggers recompilation for the new condition, with graphs cached per distinct guard combination.

flashcards.q: What is a graph break, and is it a failure?
flashcards.a: When Dynamo hits code it can't trace (data-dependent control flow on a tensor value, an untraceable library call), it falls back to eager execution for that piece and resumes tracing after -- not a crash, but Inductor can't fuse/optimize across the break, reducing compilation's benefit.

flashcards.q: What is a recompilation storm, and how is it mitigated?
flashcards.a: Highly variable input shapes trigger a new guard failure (and full recompilation) on nearly every call, so compilation cost dominates instead of amortizing. Mitigated by marking dimensions dynamic, compiling once for a range of shapes instead of one exact shape per call.

flashcards.q: What does AOTAutograd add on top of Dynamo's graph capture?
flashcards.a: It runs the forward pass once under tracing specifically to also derive the backward pass's graph ahead of time, producing a joint forward+backward representation so Inductor can apply fusion/scheduling to the backward pass with the same graph-level knowledge as the forward.

flashcards.q: What does Inductor do, and why does operator fusion matter (connect to GPU architecture)?
flashcards.a: Inductor lowers the joint graph into generated code -- fused Triton kernels for GPU, C++/OpenMP for CPU. Fusion combines a chain of ops into one kernel, paying the ~3-10us launch overhead once instead of per-op and keeping intermediates in registers/shared memory instead of redundant HBM round-trips.

It forces an explicit error at a graph break instead of a silent eager fallback, letting developers find exactly where and why performance-costing breaks occur during development rather than only inferring it from disappointing benchmarks.

flashcards.q: What does a Triton kernel let you describe, versus raw CUDA C++?
flashcards.a: Computation over a BLOCK of data (via program_id-based offsets), with the compiler handling the mapping to individual GPU threads/warps -- no manual thread indexing, shared memory management, or warp-level synchronization required, unlike raw CUDA.

flashcards.q: In a Triton kernel, why is the mask a correctness requirement, not just an optimization?
flashcards.a: Without it, tl.load/tl.store for the final partially-filled block would read/write memory past the array's actual allocated end, since blocks are launched uniformly regardless of whether n_elements divides evenly by BLOCK_SIZE -- an out-of-bounds access, not a performance issue.

flashcards.q: For n_elements=10000 and BLOCK_SIZE=1024, how many Triton grid blocks are launched, and how many trailing lanes are masked in the last block?
flashcards.a: ceil(10000/1024)=10 blocks. The 10th block covers offsets 9216-10239; only 9216-9999 (784 elements) are valid, so 240 trailing lanes are masked off.

flashcards.q: A teammate finds torch.compile makes their benchmark slower. What's the first thing to check?
flashcards.a: Whether the benchmark includes the first (compiling) call's cost -- the initial invocation pays tracing and codegen time on top of execution, which can dominate if the model only runs a handful of times.

flashcards.q: Why does Inductor generate Triton kernels rather than raw CUDA C++ for GPU targets?
flashcards.a: Triton's block-level abstraction is a smaller, more tractable code-generation target for a compiler than hand-tuned CUDA C++, while still producing kernels competitive with hand-written CUDA for most real workloads, and the output remains inspectable Python-embedded code.
